title: Ramakrishna and the last seed
hookLine: a monk presses glass to Ramakrishna's brow and tells him to go beyond even the Mother
carry: seedless: even the holiest seed is let go
last: RITAMBHARA: KNOWING IT, NOT KNOWING ABOUT IT.

cards: Bengal, the 1860s, the Kali temple at Dakshineswar near Kolkata. Its priest, Ramakrishna, loves the Goddess Kali the way a child loves his mother.

A wandering monk named Totapuri arrives, a teacher of the path of knowledge, and tells him: go beyond all forms. Ramakrishna sits to meditate, and every time, the radiant form of the Mother rises before him.

teach.b: In his own telling, as his followers recorded it, Totapuri grows stern, picks up a sliver of glass, and presses its point between Ramakrishna's eyebrows. Fix your mind here. Ramakrishna sits again.

When the Mother's form appears, he takes knowledge like a sword and cuts through it, and the last barrier falls away. His followers say he stayed absorbed for three days. That's the territory of sutra 1.51.
Tasyapi nirodhe sarva nirodhan nirbijah samadhih.
When even that is stilled, everything stilled, there is seedless absorption. Even that: the impression left by yesterday's truth-bearing wisdom, the last good groove.

When it too goes quiet, nothing is left that could sprout. Nirbija, without seed. The commentator Vyasa says the seer then rests alone, pure and free, which loops back to sutra 1.3: the seer rests in its own form.
Chapter one began with the definition of yoga and ends with yoga complete. Now the Hindu teaching, held in two hands.
Many teachers say God is both with form, saguna, and beyond all form, nirguna. Vedanta calls the deepest absorption nirvikalpa, without distinctions, a close cousin of Patanjali's seedless state.

teach.h: HE CAME BACK, STILL LOVING KALI.
teach.b: And then the part people love: Ramakrishna came back, and went on loving Kali all his life. For him, the formless and the Mother were one, the way fire and its power to burn are one.
Devotional schools weigh it differently and treasure the form itself; that's a real conversation inside Hinduism. Tomorrow, chapter two begins.

how: Hindus speak of God with form (saguna) and beyond form (nirguna), and many keep loving worship of a form alongside teaching about the formless; in classical yoga, seedless samadhi is the culmination of chapter one, studied as a map from the definition of yoga in 1.2 to its completion in 1.51.

o: absorption with no seed left that could sprout
a mind that has gone blank from tiredness
a field where nothing was ever planted

games.q: form and beyond: tap the pairs.

s: after his seedless absorption, Ramakrishna stopped worshipping Kali
he went on loving the Mother all his life; for him she and the formless were one.
seedless samadhi still rests on a subtle object
nirbija: even the last impression is stilled.
the first chapter ends where sutra 1.3 pointed: the seer resting in itself
Vyasa says the seer then rests alone, pure and free.

games.q: truth-bearing wisdom has cleared away every other impression. only its own remains. what does sutra 1.51 do with it?
o: keep it forever as the highest state.
replace it with a new seed.
games.why: when even that is stilled, everything stilled, there is seedless samadhi. the last good seed goes too.

practice: If you pray, picture the form of God you love, or a lamp's flame, and rest with it for a while. Then, without pushing it away, let the picture soften and fade, and sit holding nothing in particular, just aware.
If a thought comes, let it go without picking up a new support. It's only a taste of letting go of even the good seed.

wordCard.voice: Seedless. Nirbija samadhi, sutra 1.51: when even the last good impression is stilled, nothing remains that could sprout, and the seer rests in itself.

orig.note: Sanskrit nirbīja: seedless. the samadhi with nothing left that could sprout again.

carryVoice: Your line: seedless, even the holiest seed is let go. And Ramakrishna still came home to his Mother. Chapter one, done.
